subject: Career
title: Dormant Ties: Reactivating Old Contacts
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Dormant Ties: Reactivating Old Contacts.

hook.text: You haven't spoken in five years. Is it weird to reach out? Research says no — and it's incredibly valuable.

buildup.text: Daniel Levin's research found dormant ties provide more novel information than current contacts.

discovery.text: Old contacts have moved to new industries, roles, and networks. They bring fresh perspectives.

twist.text: People are flattered to be remembered. 'I was thinking about our work on X' is all you need.

climax.text: Reactivate five dormant ties per quarter. The ROI on these conversations is disproportionately high.

punchline.text: Old connections have new value. Reach out.

quiz.question: What did Daniel Levin's research find about dormant ties?
options: They provide more novel information than current contacts
They are less valuable than new contacts

details.summary: Dormant ties are relationships that were once active but have gone quiet over time. Research shows that reactivated dormant ties provide more novel information than current contacts because they have moved through different experiences since you last connected.
details.whyItMatters: Your richest networking resource may be people you already know but have lost touch with. Reactivation is faster and more comfortable than building new connections from scratch.
takeaways: Dormant ties provide non-redundant information unavailable in active circles
Reactivation messages feel less awkward than cold outreach
People are generally receptive to hearing from old contacts

faq.question: How do you reach out to someone you have not spoken to in years without it being awkward?
faq.answer: Reference a shared memory or the context where you originally connected, acknowledge the time gap honestly, and share a genuine reason for reconnecting. Something like 'I saw your post about X and it reminded me of our work together at Y' feels natural and warm.

faq.question: How far back can you reactivate a dormant tie before it becomes too old?
faq.answer: Studies show ties dormant for five to fifteen years still reactivate successfully, especially if there was mutual respect. The strength of the original relationship matters more than the length of the gap. Even decades-old ties can produce surprisingly warm responses.
